## Principle

Distillation is a widely used separation technique, based on a simple idea: when a liquid mixture is boiled, the vapour that is produced is not identical in composition to the liquid from which it came, but is instead richer in the component that boils more readily, the more volatile component. Condensing that vapour gives a liquid enriched in the more volatile component relative to the original mixture, and a degree of separation has been achieved. A single boiling and condensing achieves only a limited enrichment, however; the power of distillation comes from repeating the process, so that the enrichment is compounded stage by stage until the desired separation is reached.

The vapour differs in composition from the liquid because the components differ in volatility, their tendency to pass into the vapour phase. At a given temperature, the more volatile component escapes the liquid more readily and contributes a disproportionately large share of the vapour formed. As a boiling mixture is heated, the more volatile material passes over preferentially at first, which is why the vapour, and its condensate, start out enriched, while the liquid remaining in the boiler becomes steadily depleted in the volatile component and enriched in the less volatile one. Separation by distillation is therefore possible only because, and only to the extent that, the components differ in volatility; a mixture whose components were identical in volatility would yield a vapour of exactly the same composition as its liquid, and no separation could be brought about at all, however many times the operation might be repeated.

In a working distillation, the enrichment is not left to separate boilings in separate vessels. Vapour rises through the apparatus while liquid flows back down, and the two streams are brought into contact again and again along the way. Wherever rising vapour meets descending liquid, material passes between them in both directions: the less volatile component condenses out of the vapour into the liquid, while the more volatile component vaporises out of the liquid into the vapour. Each such contact therefore improves both streams at once, enriching the vapour in the volatile component as it rises, and enriching the liquid in the less volatile component as it falls. The descending liquid that makes this exchange possible is reflux, produced by condensing part of the vapour that reaches the top and returning it to the apparatus rather than drawing it all off as product.

A qualitative illustration fixes the principle. Consider a mixture of two components, one more volatile than the other, heated in a boiler until it boils. The vapour that leaves the boiler is richer in the more volatile component than the liquid remaining behind. Condensing that vapour gives a liquid of the vapour's enriched composition; boiling the condensate in its turn gives a vapour richer again. Repetition moves the collected material steadily toward the more volatile component at one end and toward the less volatile component at the other, and this compounding of many small enrichments builds a substantial overall separation from a modest difference in volatility.

## Equipment

The apparatus is the distillation column, a vertical vessel in which rising vapour and descending liquid are brought into contact. Contact is provided either by trays, horizontal plates arranged one above another up the column, or by packing, a filling of shaped material that spreads the liquid into films over a large surface. Vapour passes upward through the trays or the packing voids, bubbling through or flowing past the liquid, while liquid passes downward from tray to tray or trickles over the packing under gravity, so the exchange of the principle proceeds along the whole height.

At the foot stands a reboiler, the heat exchanger that boils the liquid collected at the bottom and generates the vapour rising through the column. At the top stands a condenser, which condenses the vapour from the topmost contact; the condensate divides into a portion returned to the column as reflux, on which the internal exchange depends, and a portion withdrawn as the overhead product, the distillate. Liquid withdrawn from the bottom is the bottoms product. The feed is introduced at an intermediate point, at a height chosen so its composition matches the streams it joins there. The section above the feed point enriches the vapour in the more volatile component; the section below strips that component from the descending liquid so it is not lost in the bottoms.

## Worked example

The column's operation can be followed through a two-component mixture, keeping to the qualitative picture of the principle. The feed enters partway up the column and divides there: its vapour joins the vapour rising from below, and its liquid joins the liquid descending from above, so that the feed is worked on by both sections of the column at once. Above the feed point, the rising vapour passes from contact to contact, giving up less volatile component to the descending liquid and taking up more volatile component in exchange. The vapour that finally reaches the condenser is therefore rich in the more volatile component, and the distillate drawn off from the condensate shares that enriched composition, although it is not, in general, the pure component, since each contact achieves only a partial exchange. Below the feed point, the descending liquid passes from contact to contact, giving up more volatile component to the rising vapour and taking up less volatile component in exchange. The liquid that finally reaches the reboiler is therefore depleted in the more volatile component, and the bottoms drawn off are enriched in the less volatile component, though again not completely pure. The two products are drawn toward opposite ends of the composition range by one internal traffic of vapour and liquid, maintained by heat supplied at the reboiler and removed at the condenser, and the separation depends on how many effective contacts the traffic passes through and how generously reflux is supplied.

## Limits

The picture presented is simplified, and its limits need stating. The treatment assumes that at every contact the vapour and liquid leaving one another have come fully into equilibrium, so each contact achieves the whole exchange equilibrium allows. Real trays and packing fall short: contact time is finite, mixing is imperfect, and the streams leave partway toward the equilibrium compositions, so a real column requires more height, or more trays, than the ideal picture suggests for the same separation. The treatment also takes the volatility difference as fixed, whereas in real mixtures it can shift with composition and operating pressure, and some mixtures form a constant-boiling combination at which vapour and liquid have the same composition; there enrichment stops, and simple distillation cannot carry the separation past it. Finally, the picture counts only compositions and contacts: it says nothing about energy consumed at reboiler and condenser, nothing about pressure drop of the rising vapour, and nothing about components that react or decompose at the boiling temperature. Within its limits the model guides; beyond them it must be supplemented before use in design.

## Principle

Distillation separates a liquid mixture by volatility. When the mixture boils, the vapour formed is richer than the liquid in the more volatile component, the component with the greater tendency to pass into the vapour. Condensation of that vapour gives a liquid enriched in the same component, and repetition of boiling and condensing compounds the enrichment until the separation required is reached. A single boiling enriches once and modestly; separation is the product of many enrichments in sequence.

Reflux makes the sequence continuous rather than batchwise. Without a descending liquid, vapour rising from the boiler would meet nothing, exchange with nothing, and leave with the composition the boiler gave it; the column would add height without adding separation. The returned liquid supplies, at every level, a stream already enriched in the less volatile component, against which the rising vapour is repeatedly corrected. The correction has a price: part of the condensed product is sent back instead of withdrawn, so the column produces less at the top than it condenses, and the separation is bought with that returned share.

Volatility difference is the whole basis of the method. At a given temperature the more volatile component escapes the liquid more readily and contributes a disproportionate share of the vapour, while the liquid left behind is depleted in that component and enriched in the less volatile one. A mixture whose components had the same volatility would give a vapour of the liquid's own composition, and no repetition would separate it.

In a working column the repetition is internal. Vapour rises and liquid descends through the same vessel, and where the two meet, material passes both ways: the less volatile component condenses from the vapour into the liquid, and the more volatile component vaporises from the liquid into the vapour. Each contact enriches both streams at once. The descending liquid is reflux, made by condensing part of the vapour at the top and returning it instead of drawing it all off as product. A qualitative example fixes the idea: vapour from a boiling two-component mixture, condensed and boiled again, gives a second vapour richer again in the more volatile component, and repetition moves material toward that component at one end of the apparatus and toward the less volatile component at the other.

## Equipment

The vessel is a vertical column. Contact inside it is provided by trays, horizontal plates stacked up the height, or by packing, a filling that spreads liquid into films over a large surface. Vapour rises through the trays or the packing voids, liquid descends over them, and the exchange of the principle proceeds along the whole height.

A reboiler at the foot boils the liquid collected there and generates the rising vapour. A condenser at the top condenses the vapour arriving from the uppermost contact, and the condensate divides: part returns to the column as reflux, and part is withdrawn as the overhead product, the distillate. Liquid withdrawn from the bottom is the bottoms product. Feed enters at an intermediate height, chosen so the feed composition matches the streams it joins. The section above the feed point enriches the vapour in the more volatile component; the section below it strips that component from the descending liquid so it is not lost in the bottoms.

Trays and packing achieve the same contact by different means. A tray holds a pool of liquid through which vapour bubbles, and the pool is renewed from above as it overflows downward. Packing holds no pools: liquid spreads over the filling and vapour passes through the voids, and contact occurs across the wetted surface. The choice between them belongs to the duty; the model of the chapter treats both alike, as providers of contacts in sequence.

## Worked example

A two-component feed enters partway up the column and divides at the feed point: its vapour joins the vapour rising from below, and its liquid joins the liquid descending from above. Above the feed point, the rising vapour passes from contact to contact, and at each contact it gives up less volatile component to the descending liquid and takes up more volatile component from it. The vapour reaching the condenser is rich in the more volatile component, and the distillate shares that composition. The distillate is not the pure component: each contact exchanges only in part, and the enrichment at the top is the sum of partial exchanges.

Below the feed point, the descending liquid passes from contact to contact, and at each contact it gives up more volatile component to the rising vapour and takes up less volatile component from it. The liquid reaching the reboiler is depleted in the more volatile component, and the bottoms are enriched in the less volatile one, again short of purity. The two products are drawn toward opposite ends of the composition range by one internal traffic, maintained by heat supplied at the reboiler and removed at the condenser. The separation achieved rests on the number of effective contacts the traffic passes through and on the reflux supplied to sustain the descending stream.

## Limits

The model of this chapter idealises every contact as an equilibrium contact, in which vapour and liquid leave one another at the compositions equilibrium allows. Real trays and packing fall short of that ideal: contact time is finite and mixing is imperfect, so a real column needs more height than the ideal picture suggests for the same separation. The model also takes the volatility difference as a fixed property of the mixture. In real mixtures it shifts with composition and with operating pressure, and some mixtures form a constant-boiling combination at which vapour and liquid have the same composition; enrichment stops there, and simple distillation does not carry a separation past that point. The model counts compositions and contacts only. Energy consumed at the reboiler and condenser, pressure drop of the rising vapour, and components that react or decompose at the boiling temperature all stand outside it.
